 Several California parents charged following their children's accidents on e-motos 
 At least 12 parents have been charged this year, the D.A. said. 
 0:34 Several California parents charged following their children's accidents on e-motos Gary Coronado/Los Angeles Times via Getty Images, FILE By Mason Leib October 22, 2026, 5:03 PM 
 Multiple California parents are facing child endangerment charges in connection with letting their children "illegally ride E-Motos," the Orange County District Attorney announced Wednesday.
 According to the district attorney's office, the charges come after multiple accidents, including one that left an 11-year-old with a broken collarbone and an arterial bleed and another in which a 13-year-old died after crashing into a light pole.
 E-motos, or electric motorcycles, are two-wheeled, off-highway motorcycles that are powered by an electric motor and have no pedals. Electric bicycles, in contrast, come with pedals and an electric motor that does not exceed 750 watts, according to the California Highway Patrol. 
 The district attorney's office announcement represents some of the 12 parents the office says it has charged since January in an effort to regulate young people on e-bikes and e-motos.
 Related Crackdowns on e-bikes and mopeds gaining steam Among those recently charged was Alex Li, who is facing a misdemeanor count of child endangerment. The district attorney's office alleges Li's 11-year-old son collided "with a pickup truck while riding his E-Moto capable of going more than 33 miles per hour in the city of Yorba Linda."
 In this Aug. 12, 2016, file photo, the Orange County Courthouse is shown in Santa Ana, Calif. Gary Coronado/Los Angeles Times via Getty Images, FILE His son suffered broken bones and an arterial bleed, the D.A.'s office said.
 Another parent, Maria Roehling, was charged with a felony count of child endangerment and an infraction for allowing a child under the age of 18 to drive a motor vehicle without a license, according to the D.A.'s office.
 According to the district attorney's office, her 9-year-old son was allegedly "speeding on his E-Moto capable of going speeds more than 47 miles per hour when he was hit by a pickup truck in Yorba Linda."

 Dan Rezmives, a father of a 12-year-old, was charged with one misdemeanor count of child endangerment, one misdemeanor count of contributing to the delinquency of a minor and an infraction for allowing a child under the age of 18 to drive a motor vehicle without a license after a police officer allegedly saw his son riding an e-moto on a city street, the D.A. said. Rezmives was allegedly on a bicycle at the time.
 The father and son were previously warned that riding the bike on city streets was illegal, the D.A.'s office said.
 Two other parents, Hulin Guo and Xiaomin Wang, were each charged with a misdemeanor count of child endangerment, one misdemeanor count of contributing to the delinquency of a minor, and an infraction for allowing a child under the age of 18 to drive a motor vehicle without a license after their 17-year-old son allegedly "led Newport Beach police on a pursuit while driving more than 40 miles an hour" on an e-moto earlier this year, according to the D.A.'s office.
 The D.A.'s office cited two prior instances in which the son allegedly had run-ins with police on E-motos, and the parents were reminded of the bikes' dangers.
 The sixth parent, Tuan Nguyen, was charged with one misdemeanor count of child endangerment after his 13-year-old son allegedly led police on a pursuit, riding up to 40 miles an hour, according to the D.A.'s office.
 "The pursuit ended when the 13-year-old crashed his Surron, capable of going up to 49 miles per hour, into the police vehicle while trying to get away," the D.A.'s office said.
 Related Growing number of trauma, brain injuries linked to e-bikes and e-scooters at 1 hospital: Study The D.A.'s office noted another man, Jose De Jesus Ramirezbarragan, was charged with one misdemeanor count of contributing to the delinquency of a minor after allegedly "allowing his 15-year-old brother to ride his E-Motorcycle."
 Ramirezbarragan's brother allegedly "began a police pursuit while driving 40 miles per hour, running red lights, and nearly crashing into several cars before losing control and crashing into several bushes," according to the district attorney's office.
 "We don't want to have to prosecute parents -- we want to save kids' lives," Orange County District Attorney Todd Spitzer said in a statement. "When parents refuse to parent and tell their kids 'no' when it comes to riding something that is dangerous and illegal, then I have no choice but to hold parents accountable and file criminal charges."
 ABC News has not yet identified attorneys for any of those charged.
 In April, the Orange County District Attorney's Office announced a mother was arrested and charged with child endangerment and accessory after the fact to a crime after her 14-year-old child allegedly hit an 81-year-old veteran while riding an e-motorcycle. The charges were later upgraded to involuntary manslaughter after the man died, authorities said. The mother has yet to enter a plea in that case.  
 The D.A.'s office said, according to the California Statewide Integrated Traffic Record System, children 11 to 14 make up 61.7% of e-moto crashes despite the fact that children under 16 are prohibited from riding e-motos.
